by.claim: RFC-002 names push-to-stage as an integration point for an external promotion system and lists implementing a change promotion system as a non-goal, so freshness of the stage branch is owned outside Argo CD. T-26443 is the consequence at that seam: in push-to-stage, auto-sync deploys whatever the stage branch last held before the external promoter moves the fresh manifests. note-1 records that the promoter on this side of the seam is still an unowned shell script, so the half of the design Argo CD delegated has no owner at all.

note-1 gates impersonation rollout on the diff story being fixed, while T-28695 notes that #24134 would make Server Side Diff the default. Because RBAC has no dry-run verb and server-side apply dry-run authorizes as `patch`, defaulting SSD before the diff path honors `destinationServiceAccounts` converts every least-privilege external cluster credential into a standing unbounded `patch` grant or a `ComparisonError`. The ordering of those two changes, not either one alone, decides whether the least-privilege boundary RFC-001 was written to create survives.

The hydrator's per-cycle commit to the hydrated branch is read by child Applications as a source change, and note-2 confirms each such push restarts the rolling sync wave, with the interim rule that hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until a debounce exists. T-27949 is that collision on the record: a repository piloting the source hydrator where every hydration commit is picked up as a source change while RollingSync loses the spec-change trigger. The hydrator commit cadence and the progressive sync step machine are coupled through the sync branch with nothing arbitrating between them.

The roadmap commits that ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented and that teardown stays a manual operator action performed one Application at a time, while the PRD's stated goal is a `deletionOrder: Reverse` that deletes children in reverse rollingSync step order and waits for each to finish. Both cannot hold: shipping the PRD retires a roadmap non-commitment that the UI/CLI/API first-class ApplicationSet item was scoped around.

T-27846 asks for progressive sync metrics because there is no wide view of where a rollout is waiting, and T-27949 reports that its ApplicationSet controller logs were at warn level so no progressive-sync transition logs were emitted at all. The observability gap is what makes the ordering designs unfalsifiable in practice: `Reverse` deletion waits for one Application to be fully deleted before the next, and nothing exposes which Application a stalled wave is waiting on, which is precisely the state T-28511 gets stuck in.

T-28239 has the commit server hold one cluster-wide GPG signing key, fail fast at startup when it is missing or invalid, and depends on the operator adding the public key to `argocd-gpg-keys-cm` and the project's `SourceIntegrity` policy. Combined with RFC-002's `repository-write` secret and its own note that push credentials probably belong in a separate namespace, the enforcing half of the design sits with the repo and cluster operators: once branch protection and SourceIntegrity are enforced against that one key, moving to per-project keys requires their consent and a coordinated rotation, not an Argo CD-side config change.
